extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, news policymakers, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and practical criteria for selecting, producing, and organizing national news so it is less distorted and more multiperspectival — emphasizing representativeness, balance, appropriate methods, audience relevance, and institutional change. Targets newsroom decision-making, resource allocation, and media-structure recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for undistorted news are value-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of undistorted news are not absolute or objective; they are based on reality and value judgments (about external reality, knowledge, truth, purposes of news, and ideas of the good nation and society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that accusations of distortion (e.g., ideological bias or reliance on official sources) rest on differing value assumptions; choosing or defending a standard is a political act and requires taking sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts as answers to questions (question-framing matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual 'news' depends on what questions are asked and on the concepts and empirical methods used; different questions, concepts, or methods produce different facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the questions being asked and the methods/concepts used to produce a report; evaluate news partly by whether the questions chosen are the 'right' ones for the purpose defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of methods to journalistic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic empirical methods aim mainly at description for a lay audience and are different from social-science methods aimed at explanation and prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether journalistic methods used (speed, selection, summary) are appropriate given the purpose (description vs explanation) and the audience; recognize limits (time, budget) and when deeper social-science methods or follow-up analysis are warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience relevance and communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: News must consider the audience and how it should be informed; journalists serve a lay audience and must present findings as interestingly and compactly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance depth and comprehensibility: prioritize presentation formats and vocabularies that the target audience can understand, and consider whether expert-level (explanatory-predictive) material is suitable or needs translation for lay readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between explanatory (expert) and dramatic (popular) news
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory-predictive news (expert news) is desirable for understanding but may not be appropriate for or accepted by a lay audience; popular dramatic news attracts attention but can be superficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide editorially how much explanatory depth to pursue given audience expectations and democratic objectives; avoid simply blaming the audience for preferring dramatic news without addressing underlying inequalities in access to expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance and study of harmful exaggeration (highlighting effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting and dramatic construction can exaggerate external reality (as measured by empirical standards) and may harm audiences if they act on distorted impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with highlighting; commission or consult research on effects of exaggeration; encourage audiences' self-protective 'discounting' but seek ways to reduce demonstrably deleterious exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness: present as many perspectives as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally the news should be omniperspectival (present all perspectives), but realistically it should be multiperspectival — presenting and representing as many perspectives as feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for breadth in sourcing and topics so the symbolic arena includes diverse perspectives; accept practical limits but strive to expand beyond the present near-uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness: include all sectors and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: News should enable all sectors of nation and society to place their actors and activities in the symbolic arena — reporting opinions and activities from groups defined by age, income, education, ethnicity, religion, and social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories and sourcing that let ordinary people from varied sectors appear and speak about what matters to them; measure representativeness by diversity of sectors and roles covered, not only by elite sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-up coverage (add grassroots perspectives to top-down news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectival news should add a bottom-up view alongside current top-down approaches: e.g., accompany federal/corporate policy coverage with reactions from citizens across walks of life who are affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reactions and lived-experience reporting from intended and unintended beneficiaries, victims, bystanders; expand beats and reporting resources to reach decentralized, harder-to-access sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Output news: emphasize how plans/programs work in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: News should report how the plans and programs of national and nationwide agencies have worked out in practice for intended and unintended beneficiaries, victims, bystanders, and the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact by output indicators (actual outcomes) rather than just statements of intent; follow up on implementation and effects rather than only reporting announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service news: provide personally relevant information for specific sectors/roles
rubrics_metrics.description: News should emphasize service news that gives personally relevant information for specific population sectors and roles (e.g., poor people need news about welfare and jobs policies; homeowners need different housing news than tenants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate coverage to issues that matter to particular audiences and craft practical, role-specific reporting rather than assuming one-size-fits-all national stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize balance and source-mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater balance requires journalists to be knowledgeable about the universe of all possible sources and perspectives and to choose sources to represent those not recently heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a mapping of sources and perspectives (by social scientists, statisticians, journalists where possible); in the interim, actively seek and include more currently unrepresented sources and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redefine 'importance' to weight sector relevance and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should redefine importance considerations to give greater weight to information important to various sectors of the population and less to 'nation and society' as abstract units; stories grow in importance by number of affected sectors or drastic impact on a few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt impact/output-based measures when judging importance; consider whether actions/statements of officials significantly affect identifiable sectors and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce primacy of novelty/peg in story selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectivalism would require giving up some selection criteria like novelty and immediate topical peg, as including many perspectives makes constant breaking news impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for periodic features, longer stories, and analyses instead of daily retelling of headlines; editors may trade immediacy for representativeness and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change story format: longer pieces, organization of multiple perspectives, and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When several perspectives must be taken into account, stories will become longer and require organization, relation, and interpretation — leading to more frequent news analyses and possibly more journalistic commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt formats and production schedules to permit longer analytic pieces, capsule biographies, documentary techniques, and translated expert vocabularies to preserve audience interest and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruiting and training journalists for perspectival sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be recruited and trained to deal with a much larger number of scattered sources, to develop sensitivity and empathy with diverse sources, and to establish beats among different population sectors; greater heterogeneity in staff backgrounds is likely essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create beats for sectors/roles, hire reporters with varied life experiences, and train reporters in outreach, empathy, and the ability to translate perspectives for broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as intent achieved through perspectival diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity remains necessary but attains new meaning: story selectors can be objective only by choosing news from several perspectives and by setting aside their personal political values in story selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate roles (objective journalists, analysts, commentators); preserve impartial story selection while allowing explicit ideological diversity in commentary; require editorial routines that ensure inclusion of multiple perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical sourcing: recognize and disclose source interests
rubrics_metrics.description: As sources multiply, reporters must be aware of overt and covert interests that shape what sources tell and omit; these source 'axes' directly affect what becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vet and contextualize sources, disclose relevant interests and limitations, and seek corroboration or countervailing perspectives to prevent unbalanced reliance on interested parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-opinion measurement focused on salience and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where public-opinion polls are used, they should ask people what is on their minds rather than only approval/disapproval of policies; reporting should emphasize opinions across sectors/roles rather than numerical majorities alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design polls to surface agenda salience and cross-sectional differences; report poll findings by sector/role and highlight minority but sectorally important views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and resource changes: larger newshole and media structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectival news requires more newshole and different media structures (centralized expansion, decentralized array, or a two-tier model combining central and audience-specific media) to handle greatly increased reporting demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a two-tier model (central multiperspectival media complemented by smaller second-tier outlets serving homogeneous audiences), plan for subsidies or new funding models, and allocate resources for original reporting and reanalysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical modesty: implement a modest degree of multiperspectivism
rubrics_metrics.description: Given constraints, central media should adopt a modest degree of multiperspectivism — more balance and representativeness but within limits of newshole and organizational capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize multiperspectivalism by ensuring more unrepresented sources appear, by elevating balance considerations in routine editorial judgment, and by incrementally adjusting beats, formats, and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about limits and editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Because no single news organization can include all perspectives, choosing what to include/exclude is inevitably political and requires journalists to take sides and be transparent about those editorial choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make editorial rationales visible (e.g., why certain perspectives were included or omitted), clarify the intended purposes of coverage, and allow room for commentators and advocacy journalists to express explicit values while keeping news selection impartial.
